method: A reverse DNS name is the address written backwards under a fixed suffix: IPv4 octets reversed below in-addr.arpa, IPv6 hex digits reversed one per label below ip6.arpa. The page masks the address to the prefix length first and reports any host bits it cleared. For IPv4 a /24 owns the three-label zone d.c.b.in-addr.arpa and the last octet is the relative owner name, so all 256 names are listed. A prefix longer than /24 covers part of one /24: the page names the RFC 2317 child zone start-end.d.c.b.in-addr.arpa and emits one CNAME per address in the parent zone so resolvers follow the delegation. A /32 is reported as one full owner name. A prefix shorter than /24 spans several /24 zones, which are listed (at most 64) rather than merged into a zone that does not exist. For IPv6 the zone is the reversed network nibbles of the prefix; a prefix that is not a multiple of 4 is rounded down to the nearest nibble boundary and the status line says so, because delegation happens on nibble boundaries. Relative IPv6 owners are the remaining address nibbles in reverse. PTR lines are listed while the block holds at most 256 addresses; larger blocks show the apex and the exact name count. The PTR target is trimmed, must be a syntactically valid DNS name of at most 253 characters, and gets a trailing dot so it is not read relative to $ORIGIN. The page emits $ORIGIN and record lines only: no SOA, no NS, no serial and no DNSSEC, because those need a server and contact it cannot know. It performs no lookup, so it cannot tell whether a zone is delegated or a PTR record answers; everything is computed locally with no network access, storage or uploads.
